Creator: Will-makers of the Province of York (the wills themselves); selected and edited for the Surtees Society by James Raine and John William Clay (as the host record lists the editors)

Publication Date: 1869

Provenance note: Header prepended; the OCR text follows unchanged apart from this header. Google scanning notice left in place. OCR sampled at the opening, the middle and the end: mostly readable; Latin abstracts of wills and English notes with some misread letters. Nothing corrected, re-spaced or retyped.
Content note: Volume IV of the Surtees Society's selection of York wills: the wills, in Latin and in English, with the editors' preface and long notes on the testators and their families, and an index. The wills in this volume are mostly of the 1460s to 1509. The will-makers' own words, in the form the registry kept. PREFACE. 



The fourth volume of the Testamenta Eboracensia 
covers a period of about twenty-five years, and brings 
the series down to the commencement of the reign 
of Henry VIII. It has been found impossible to 
travel more quickly over a field which is so crowded 
with interesting documents. At the same time, the 
Editor has not scrupled to abridge his materials where 
curtailment was practicable, and all formal and 
valueless details have been generally discarded. 

The next volume ought to extend, if possible, over 
the reign of Henry VIII., but the reader will find 
that after the beginning of the sixteenth century the 
Wills preserved at York become gradually less in- 
teresting. At the same time, as evidences for the 
genealogist, they lose not a tittle of their value; nay, 
that value increases as we near the period at which 
the Heralds began to hold their Visitations. But we 
may look in vain for the quaint verbiage of the pre- 
ceding reigns, and for the minute enumeration of the 
testator's wealth and substance which was previously 
so common. 

The question has been asked more than once, Why 
is there not a glossary to each of these volumes of 



VI PREPACK. 



Wills ? The reason is this. In a work peculiarly 
devoted to genealogy it seemed inadvisable to intro- 
duce among the illustrative notes any explanations 
of dialects or language. The genealogical notes of 
themselves take up all the space that could be spared 
for illustration. And no glossary has been appended 
to these volumes, because it id the intention of the 
Society before long to take this subject in hand on a 
much larger scale. Great preparations have already 
been made for a glossary of northern words in use 
prior to the reign of Queen Anne. To construct this, 
the greater part of the volumes that the Society has 
published will be laid under contribution, and the 
work will be supplemented and illustrated by MS. 
evidences of undoubted authority, and also, in some 
cases, by the printed works of northern writers. 

Por the notes to which the initials of R. H. S. are 
appended the Editor is indebted to the kindness and 
16cal research of Mr. Skaife. That gentleman has 
also added to the value of this volume by a capital 
index, which he has prepared with his customary 
skill. Nor must Messrs. Hudson and Buckle be 
passed over. They are always ready to throw open 
the treasures in their office for the benefit of this 
Society, and the Editor has always been welcomed by 
them with unvarying courtesy and attention. 

J. R. 

York, October, 1869.

Ilie Hildjards are a very ancient Yorkshire family. A piece of evidence has 
occurred to me in the shape of a suit in the Ecclesiastical Court at York in 1370, 
which places their early history on a new and satisfactory footing. It turns on 
the legality of a marriage between two cousins, which is best represented in a short 
tabular pedigree. One of the witnesses says that the ** stirps " of the family 
came from Hildyard in Essex. The accuracy of this account is confirmed b^ 
that invaluable piece of Yorkshire history, the Liber de Melsa. (See vol. ii. 
218-19.)

XIV. THE WILL OF SIR RALPH GREYSTOCK KNT,, BAROK OF 

GREYSTOCK. 

[Reg. Rotherham, 334^.] 

May 27, 1487. Badulphus, dominus de Grastok* et Weme. 
Sep. in cancello monasterii Sanctae Trinitatis de Kirkham, coram 
altari. Priori et conventui dicti monasterii, pro sepultara mea, 
die obitus mei, ac pro decimis meis oblitis, cs. Priori dicti 

* A hitherto nnknown will of the head of the great baronial house of Grey- 
stock. For an account of the family, see Hodgson's Northumberland, ii. part ii. 
378-9 ; Coll. Top. ii. 160-1. The evidences at York add materially to the informa- 
tion there ^iren. 

The will of his, the testator's, father, who died in 1436, is in Wills and 
Inv. i. 84-6. 

In 1435 the testator married Elizabeth daughter of William Lord Fitzhngh. 
(Test. Ebor. iii. 327-8.) The marriage licence shows the affinity of the two 
contracting parties. He is said to hare married, secondly, Elizabeth, daughter of 
John Terell, (Coll. Top. ii. 160,) but his widow's name was Beatrix (Hatcliffe), 
and she re-married Robert Constable, esq., serieant-at-law, in 1490. (Test. 
Ebor. iii. 365.) She suryired him, and, taking the vows of chastity in 1501-2, 
(Ibid. 363) made her will in 1505. This is printed afterwards. 

The testator was buried in the noble monastery of Eirkham, of which, by 
inheritance, he was the founder. The chaplets of Greystock still surmount the 
beautiful gateway of the Priory. The ancient numor of Hinderskelf, in which 
the Greystocks lived, has now changed its name to Castle-Howard. 

According to the Coll. Top. the testator had many children. John, one of his 
sons, made a splendid alliance with Cecily daughter of William Herbert, Earl of 
Pembroke. (Test. Ebor. iii. 349.) This was not known before. 

Richard Greystock, another of his. sons, took holy orders. On March 10, 
1463-4, he was collated by Archbishop Booth to the rectory of Wheldrake, which 
he resigned in Feb. 1486-7. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 73b.) On May 7, 1465, the 
Dean and Chapter of York, sede vacante, granted him letters dimissory. (Beg. 
$ede vacant^, 455 b), and on April 7 in the next year he was allowed to be absent 
from his living two years. (Keg. Geo. Neville, 53 a.) On Dec. 3, 1481, he was 
instituted to the rectory of Brompton, in Pickering Lythe (Reg. Rotherham, 158 a.) 
which he held till his death. (Ibid. 92 b.) On Feb. 15, 1475-6, he was installed 
prebendary of Welton Brinkhall, at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 229.) On Feb. 24, 
1486-7, he was made succentor canonicorum at York (Reg. Rotherham, 1026.), 
and he died holding that office in 1496. 

The following notices are illustrative of the Greystock pedigree. Nov. 25, 
1346, nuncupative will of Elizabet de Graystok. To be buried in the church of 
Butterwick. Sir Ralph de Hastings, knt. sen., and Richard de Neville, lector 
of Scotton, executors. They renounce, and William de Kelk administered. 
(Reg. Zouche, 305 J.) She was a Neville, and the widow of Robert fitz Ralph, 
lord of Graystock. According to what is called the Greystock Roll, which is 
now before me, " Iste Robertas scpultus est apud Botyrwyk." At Butterwick 
there is an effigy of a knight, which may perhaps commemorate him. Some 
modem churchwardens, anxious to leave a memorial of their ta.ste and skill 
even more striking than usual, have set the statue up against the chancel wall, 
whilst, above the head of the figure, they have made an arch of two fragments 
of the rib of a whale. To add to their beauty the bones are duly white-washed I 

On Aug. 3, 1473, administration of Isabella lady Greystock, late wife of Sir 
Ralph Greystock, knt., was granted to Sir Henry Vavasour, knt., Thomas 
Thwaites, and William Scargill, sen., esqs, (Reg. Test. iv. 199*.) Perhaps she 
was a wife of the testator.

Ampleforth, at York. (Ibid. 7 a.) On Feb. 14, seq., he was collated to the pre- 
bend of St. Andrew at Beverley. (Ibid. 11 b.) On Aug. 18, 1477, he was

identit]^ — a monk could not make a will.

(Thoroton'B Notts, 57.) His wife was Alice, daaghter of John Booth, and sister 
of archbishop William Booth. She died Sept. 9, 1470. (Ibid.) 

In 1456 the testator Sir Gerrase married Alice, daughter of Thonuis Neville, 
esq., and widow of Richard Thnrland of Nottingham. (Test Ebor. iii. 334.) In 
1483 he married another widow, Agnes, widow of Sir Walter Griffith. (Ibid. 347.) 
Her will occurs afterwards. (See Test. Ebor. iii. 269.) Sir Gervase left many 
children, and was a worthy representative of his illnstrions family. He died at 
the Friars Preachers, London, May 12th, 1491, and was interred at Clifton. 
(Thoroton, 671.) He was esquire of the body to Edward IV., and Knight of the 
Bath. 

Robert Qifton, brother of Sir Gervase, was archdeacon of the East Riding. 
On May 3rd, 1454, he was collated to the stall of North Muskham at Southwell, 
on the resignation of Robert his father, as proctor of Gervase his brother. (Reg. 
Wm. Booth, 31 b.) A nice specimen of archbishop Booth's nepotism ! (Gervase 
Clifton was collated to it Nov. 4, 1463. Ibid. Si a. He was the testator, and in 
no orders whatever.) On May 28, 1463, Robert Clifton was collated to the pre- 
bend at St. Michael's altar at Beverley (Reg. Wm. Booth, 5iki.) ; and, on March 
13, 1463-4, his uncle collated him to the archdeaconry of the East Riding. (Ibid. 
68a.) At this time he was only an acolyte, and on Sept. 12, 1464, he had leave 
to proceed to the higher orders. (Ibid. 223^.) The archdeacon died young and 
intestate. On Aug. 27, 1467, administration to his effects was granted to £>bert 
Hill and William Heseham. (Reg. Test. iv. 238 a.) 

t Even the names of some of these children have not been previously known. 

Gamaliel Clifton was a distinguished man. At his father's death he must have 
been very young. On Feb. 17, 1499-1500, Mr. Gamaliel Clifton, scholar and 
bachelor of laws, of Clifton, had letters dimissory. (Reg. Rotherham, 267 b.) 
On July 30, 1500, he was instituted to the rectory of Hawton, Notts, on the pre- 
sentation of Thomas Molyneux, es^. (MS. Cotton, Galba, E. x., 135 a.) On Aug. 
3 in the same year he was admitted to the stall of Wistow at York. (Acta 
Capit. Ebor.) On Sept. 19 and Dec. 19, 1500, he was ordained deacon and priest, 
respectively, on the title of his living and stall. (Reg. Arundel at Lichfield, 292.) 
On Feb. 12, 1508-9, he was instituted to the rectory of Wilford, Notts, on the 
presentation of Robert Clifton, of Clifton, esq. (Reg. Savage, 6a.) On 8th 
August, 1522, he was appointed canon of Windsor by patent, a post which he 
held till 1541. (Le Neve, iii. 392.) In 1525 he became prebendary of Pratum 
Minors at Hereford, which he resigned on May 16, 1529, for the prebend of 
Colwell. (Ibid. i. 499-625.) On 5 Jul^, 1529, he was elected dean of Hereford. 
(Ibid. i. 477.) This office, together with the rectory of West Ildesley, Berks, and 
other posts and dignities, he held till his death. His will is dated April 28, 
1541, and, dying in that year, he was buried in Hereford cathedral. (Willis, ii. 
635.) He proceeded bachelor of civil law at CJambridge, and subsequently doctor, 
and supplicated for incorporation at Oxford in 1521. He was of high repute as 
a canonist, and was one of the lawyers who were concerned with the divorces 
between* Henry VIII. and Katharine of Arragon and Anne of Cleves. (Ath. 
. Cant. i. 78, 533. Fiddes's Life of Wolsey, appendix, 203.) 

Silvan Clifton was instituted to the rectory of Clifton on May 30th, 1506 (Reg. 
Savage, 61 a.), and gave it up in 1531 for Norbiton in the diocese of Winchester. 

Heiekiah Clifton lived at Bnrton Agnes in Yorkshire, and will occur after- 
wards.

He was a member of a Lancashire family, a branch really of the Traffords, 
which afterwards produced two noted men, William Chaderton, bishop of Chester,, 
and Lawrence Chaderton, one of the translators of the Bible. (F.R.R.) He came 
into Yorkshire with archbishop BooUi. It is no easy matter to enumerate the 
offices that he held. 

On April, 1460, at a prirate and special ordination he was ordained acolyte in 
the chapel at Scrooby by John Green, bishop of the Isles, he being of the diocese 
of Coyentry and Lichfield. (Beg. Wm. Booth, adfinem,) On 20th bept. seg[. he was 
made snb-deacon. (Ibid.) On April 27th, 1462, on the resignation of the prelate 
just mentioned, he was instituted to the vicarage of Blyth, which he resigned in 
August %eq, (^Ibid. 96 ^.) On Sept. 20, 1462, he was instituted to the rectoiy of 
Broughton, Sir Robert Clifton presenting him. (Ibid. 99 a.) This, on June 20, 
1470, he exchanged for the vicarage of Kirkby Lonsdale. (Reg. archid. Rich- 
mond, 60 A.) (hi Oct. 7, 1465, he was made archbishop NeviUe^s receiver for 
Hexhamshire (Reg. Geo. Neville, 40^), and on Nov. 6, 1466, being that prelate's 
chaplain, he was instituted to the rectory of Hockerton, Notts (Ibid. 356), which 
he resigned in Oct. 1470. On June 26th, 1473, he was instituted to the rectory 
of Staunton, Notts (Ibid. 153a), which he resigned in July, 1478, receiving a 
pension of seven marks per annum out of it. On Jan. 6, 1474-5, he was collated 
to the stall of South Muskham at Southwell, resigning the Sacrist's prebend 
there. (Ibid ii. 3 a.) On Feb. 10, 1475-6, he was collated to the stall of North- 
well, 3rd part, there. (Ibid. 236.) On Nov. 10, 1476, he was collated to a moietv 
of the stall of Oxton cum Crophill in the same church, of which he was a resi- 
dential. (Reg. L. Booth, 9 a.) On March 29, 1478, he exchanged his prebend 
at St. Katharine's altar in Beverley minster for the stall of Stretton, at Salisbury 
(Reg. Lanr. Booth, 11-12), and on Aug. 26, 1478, he was appointed master or 
warden of Sibthorpe college. (Ibid. 46a.] From 1475 to 1482 he held the stall 
of Welton Ryval at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 234.) 

During the reign of Richard III. Chaderton was in high favour with the king, 
and preferments were showered upon him. On Au^. 14, 1483, he was instituted 
to the rectory of Calverton, Bucks, of the king's gift. (MS. Harl. 433, 143, and 
Lipscombe's Bucks, iv. 86.) The same monarch made him clerk of the hanaper, 
treasurer, and receiver of the chamber, dean of the free chapel at Barking; and 
granted him the wardship and marriage of William, son and heir of George 
Bothe; the farm of the Temple near Marlborough; the lands of William Coling- 
boume, and the manor of Knesall, Notts. (MS. Harl., ut supra^ 32 a, 365, 805, 
95a, 99a, 103a, 104 5.) In Feb. 1492-3 he was made archdeacon of Chester 
(Le Neve, i. 567), an office which he held during his life. At his death he held 
two other archdeaconries, that of Salisbury, to which he was collated probably 
in 1483 (Le Neve, ii. 625), and that of Totnes at Exeter, to which he was ap 
pointed in 1491. (Le Neve, 1. 403.) 

His list of preferments is not yet done. In Aug. 1484 he was collated to the 
prebend of Cadington Minor at London, which he held till he died. (Le Neve, 
li. 372; Newcourt, i. 131.) On Sept. 25, 1484-6, he was instituted, at the king's 
presentation, to the rectory of Almondbury. (Ibid. 117 a.) On Jan. 2, 1484-5, 
he was collated to the prebend of Thorp at Ripon. (Reg. Rotherham, 97 5.) 
On April 8, 1485, he was collated to the stall of Dunham at Southwell, resigning 
tiiat of Oxton. (Ibid. 98 5.) In June, 1485, he was made prebendary of Nassing- 
ton at Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 193.) On Jan. 30, 1487-8, he was collated to the 
stall of St. Andrew at Beverley. (Reg. Rotherham, 103a.) On July 7tfa, 1491, 
he was made a collector of the subsidy for the expedition to France. (Foed. xii. 
446.) From 1492 to 1493 he was vicar of AUhallows Barking (Newcourt, i.

* The testator was a doctor of laws, a scholar, and an ecclesiastic of wealth 
and high position. 

On Nov. 9, 1459, he became warden of All Sonls, Oxford, having been a little 
before the principal of the halls of St George and Woodcock, and moderatcnr of 
the school of Cfcsarean law. In the same jear he was presented by his college 
to the rectory of Stanlake, and from 1459-60 to 1464 he was rector of Elmeley 
(Hist Univ. Oxon. iv. 268. Newcoort, i. 210.) On August 21, 1460, he was 
collated to the rectory of Roding Alta in Essex (Newconrt ii. 60n, which he 
held for a short time. On Feb. 9, 1465-6, he became prebendary of Empingham 
at Lincoln, and continued so for nine years. (Le ^leve, ii. 147.) In 1466 his 
college presented him to the rectory of Treng. (Hist. Univ. Oxon. iv. 268.) 

Whilst Foteman was warden of All Souls, George Neville, bidiop of Exeter, 
was chancellor of the University. When that prelate was translated to York 
in 1466, Foteman found in him a mnniiicent patron, and followed him into the 
North. In that vear Foteman resigned several of his southern benefices, vis., 
the wardenship of All Souls, the rectory of Chelmsford, and the stall of Sneat- 
ing at London. (Newcourt, i. 210.) At York he was a canon in residence, and 
held the following posts in the church of York ; the stall of Weighton to which 
he was collated Feb. 22, 1466-7. (Reg. Geo. Neville, Ba.) This he gave up whra 
admitted on Sept 25, 1470, to that of Bamby. (Acta Capit. 9hS annv.) On 
Sep. 25, 1470, he was made archdeacon of Cleveland (Ibid.), and was so until 
14S4. On Jan. 29, 1474-5, he was collated to the stall of Strensall, which he 
held till he died. (Reg. Geo. Neville, ii. ia.)

He held other preferment in the diocese. On March 30, 1467, archhiabop 
Keville made Poteman provoet of Beverley, in which ofiSce he died. (Ibid Bb.) 
He also instituted him on Jan. 2, 1465-6, to the rectory of Settrington, which, 
with the stall of Bambj, he gave np in 1470, in exchange for the archdeaconry 
of Cleveland. (Ibid. 27 b.) The archbishop admitted him to a prebend at Hem- 
ingborongh on Dec. 27, 1466. (Ibid 87 b.) On Nov. 15, 1468, ne became vicar-

general. (Ibid. 90a et seq.) Indeed it is impossible to examine the register of 
archbishop Neville widiont seeing that the management of the diocese of York 
was chiefly entrusted to Poteman's care. 

After the death of archbishop Neville, Poteman was not forgotten by his suc- 
oessors in the see. On Feb. 14, 147 7-8, he was made prebendary of Nunwick at Ripon 
(Reg. Laur. Booth, 13 a), and master of the hospital of B.M. Magdalen in the same 
town in July, 1479. (Ibid. 52 J.) Thrice, viz. on 30th Aug. 1478, 18th Sept. 1480, 
and in Aug. 1485, he was made official of the court of York (Reg. Booth and 
Rotherham), and once, on Sept. 18, 1480, he was made vicar-general to arch- 
bishop Rotherham. (Reg. Rotherham, la, b.) On Jan. 13, 1484-5, he was made 
archdeacon of the East Riding (Ibid. 98a), an office which he filled during his 
life. On March 16, 1471-2, Poteman was appointed to treat with the commis- 
sioners of Scotland about a truce. (Foed.xi. 748, Rot. Scot. ii. 434.) On May 16, 
1473, he had the charge of punishing those who broke the truce. (Ibid. xi. 776, 
Rot Scot. ii. 437.) On Feb. 20, 1474-5, he was made a commissioner to settle 
the dispute about the fisheries in the Esk. (Rot. Scot ii. 451.) On Aug. 20, 
1484, he was made a justice of peace and quorum for Ripon. (Reg. Rotherham, 
214a.) And on Sept. 12, 1488, he was again appointed an ambassador to treat 
for peace with Scotland. (Rot. Scot. ii. 487.)

may hear service, and have the usual rites performed in a chapel within the 
manor house of the said Brian at Cowthorpe, until the new church is finished. The 
commissioners report favourably, and on Feb. 13, 1456-6, the archbishop sanctions 
the scheme, and grants an indulgence of 40 days to all those who assist the work. 
(Beg. Wm. Booth, 184-6.) On Aug. 17, 1468, the archbishop desired his suffragan, 
John bishop of Fhilippolis, to consecrate the new church, with a similar indul- 
gence. (Ibid. 368-9.)

of the king's house (Fuller's Univ. Cant. 90); Master of the Rolls in 1483 (MS. 
Harl. 433 152), with a grant of two pipes of Gascoigne wine each year. (Foed. 
xii. 208.) On July 18, 1483, he was made archdeacon of Colchester, and acted 
as such till he died. (Newcourt, i. 90.) On Sept. 20, 1484, he was made an 
ambassador to negotiate a peace with Scotland (Feed. xii. 235 ; Rot. Scotise, ii. 
465.) On Aug. 1, 1485, he was appointed keei)er of the privy seaL (Feed. xii. 
272; Dugd. Chron. 72.) There is a brief notice of him in Foss's Judges, iv. 
485-6, from which it appears that he was a prebendary of St. Stephen's, West? 
minster, a trier of petitions in parliament, and one of the masters in chancery. 

Barrow's will is at Doctors' Commons, but I have no notes from it. He died 
in 1501. He gave £240 toward the building of St. Mary's, Cambridge (Fuller's 
Univ. Cant. SS.) He left certain rents to the university for keeping his exequies 
(MS. Baker, at Cambridge, xxiv. 26).

♦ " Ricardus de York, merchannt," was admitted to the freedom of the city of 
York, by purchase, in 1456. He was chamberlain in 1460, sheriff in 1465-6, lord 
mayor in 1469 and 1482, and was elected M.P. in 1473, 1482 (Dec. 13), 1483 
(Oct. 24), 1483-4 (Jan. 16), 1486, 1488 (Dec. 31), and 1490. 

In 1462, Richard York and his wife became members of the merchants' gnild, 
and he was master of that gnild, and of the company of merchants and merceis, 
in 1475. On January 15, 1466-7, being then mayor of the Staple of Calais, he 
was one of the guests at the great installation feast of arcnbidiop Neville. 
When King Henry VII. visited York in July 1487, " in the Vigill of Saint Peter 
callid Advincle," he "dubbed my Lord Maier, called William Todde, and 
Richard York, alderman, knightes,*' they being the only citizens on whom he 
conferred that honour. — R. H. S. Sir Richard died in April 1498, and was 
buried in the church of St. John in Micklegate, where were many memorials of 
him and his family. Some of them still remain there. 

Sir Richard left a large family behind him. His first wife is said to have been 
Joan Mauleverer, and she, no doubt, was the mother of his children.

Several other members of the family of Worsley were connected with the coun^ 
of York and its archbishops. 

On March 30, 1462, Benjamin Worsley, the archbishop's servant, was made 
keeper of the manor of Scrooby. (Reg. Wm. Booth, li2b.) After his death, his 
widow took the veil. (Test £bor. iii. 346.) 

On Dec. 9, 1458, John Worsley, commissary-general of the court of York, was 
collated to a stall in St Sepulchre's chapel, York. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 45.) This 
he exchanged on Nov. 23, 1465, with William Betson for the prebend of 
** Kynwaston, alias Stonhall " in the royal chapel at Wolverhampton. (Reg. Geo. 
Neville, 3.) On March 9, 1460-1, he was instituted to the vicarage of Felkirk. 
(Reg. Wm. Booth, 407a.) 

On June 28, 1452, on the cession of William Worsley, Thomas Worsley was 
collated to the stall of Tachbrook at Lichfield, and he held it until 1501. (Le 
Neve, i. 629). On March 3, 1461-2, he was collated to the stall of Normanton 
at Southwell, in the person of Seth Worsley, esq., his proctor. (Reg. Wm. Booth, 
54.) He gave this up when, on the 13th of March, 1463-4, he was collated to 
the stall at the altar B.M.V. at Beverley. (Ibid. 58, 58 J.) On May 28, 1464, 
Thomas Worsley, canon of Beverley, was ordained deacon at York. (Ibid.)

In 1445, Mr. John Lancastre clerk, son of John Lancastre, tailor, York, was 
admitted to his freedom. Bobert Lancastre, clerk, son of John Lancastre, tailor, 
was liying in 1447. In 1457, John Lancastre merchant, son of William Lancastre 
d.erk, was made free. In 1472, Mr. Nicholas Lancastre, clerk and merchant, and, 
in 1478, Bichard Lancastre clerk, sons of John Lancastre merchant, became 
freemen bj patrimony. The above Nicholas was admitted into the Merchants' 
Gnild in 1472, and was constable of the Merchants' Company 1474. As '* Nicholas 
Lancastere, in ntroque jnre baccalaorens," he was elected common clerk of the 
city of York on Feb. 3rd, 1476-7, vice Bichard Derwentwater, and he resigned 
th&t office in 1480. In 1483, he occurs as one of the king's council (Extracts 
from York Becords, 207). Nicholas Lancastre, LIj.D. was elected an alderman 
April 10th, 1484, filled the office of Lord Mayor in 1485 and 1493, was retomed 
M.P. for the city of York October 16th, 1487, and died in 1601. In his wiU, 
dated January lOth, 1500-1 [Pro. Sept 1, 1501] , he desires to be buried in the 
church of St. Michael-le-BelErey.— B. H. S.

On Jannaiy Slst, 1486-7, William Todd was re-elected alderman, and a few 
days afterwards was chosen lord mayor. During his year of office he repaired, 
at his own cost, a considerable portion of the city walls adjoining Fishergate 
Bar, and, on Jnly SIst, received the honour of knighthood from King Henry the 
Seventh. On December 3l8t, 1488, he was elected M.F., and he was again 
retomed in 1490. 

In 1465 William Todd and his wife were admitted into the Merchants' Guild, 
and he was constable of the Merchants' Company in 1471, 1472 and 1475, and 
master in 1477 and 1478. 

Sir William Todd was thrice married. The name of his first wife, who was 
living in 1465, is not known. His second wife was Margaret, widow of Thomas 
Ecki&ell of Scarborough. In her will, dated 30th July, 1483 (Pro. 23 Sep. 1483), 
she desires to be buried in the monastery at Whitby. (Reg. Test. v. 199.) The 
third wife of Sir William Todd was Elizabeth Eland, of Hull. Licence to 
marry them was granted to the curate of the chapel of the Holy Trinity, Hull, 
January 24th, 1484-6. (Test. Ebor. iii. 349.) R. H. S.

This note bears the initials of my lamented friend, Mr. J. R. Walbran, of 
Ripon, who died very recently. His death is the greatest loss which English 
archaeology has sustained since that of Mr. Hunter. I shall speak elsewhere of 
his merits and his works.

James Harrington was the son of Robert Harrington and Isabel Balderston. 
(Hunter's South Yorkshire ii. 402. Whitaker's Richmondshire, ii. 261.) In his 
early life he was in some political trouble, for he dared to be a Yorkist when the 
Lancastrian interest was too paramount. On May 27, 1496, he was instituted to 
the recto^ of Badsworth on the presentation of Thomas earl of Derby, con- 
stable of England, and Joan, widow of Sir John Pilkington, knt. (Reg. Rother- 
ham, 134^.) This he held for his life. On July 2l8t, 1497, the archbishop 
granted him letters dimissory. (Ibid. 262 d.) On Oct. 29, 1601, he was instituted 
to the rectory of Tankersley, which he also held during his life. (Reg. Savage, 
10 h.). On Aug. 20, 1606, he was collated to a stall in St. Sepulchre chapel at 
York (Ibid. 29J.), which he gave up in 1611. On Jan. 27, 1506-7, he was 
collated to the stall of Husthwaite at York. (Ibid. 30 a.) On July 13th, ««^., 
he was made subdean (Ibid. 31 a.); and on Jan. 29th in the following year, by a 
rapid and most unprecedented step, he was advanced to the deanery. (Acta 
Capit. Ebor.) On March 30th, 1609, he was made prebendary of Bugthorpe. 
(Reg. Bainbridge, 31 b.) 

Dean Harrington did not hold his high office for a long time, and he suffered 
from ill-health before he died. On Dec. 2nd, 1610, he is excused by the 
chapter from coming to the Minster during his greater residence, as he is so ill 
that he cannot go up to or leave his stall. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) He was buried 
in his cathedral on the festival of the Innocents, 1612, and on April 26, 1613, 
Mr. Thomas Wolsey, his successor, administered to his effects. (Ibid.) Among 
the fabric accounts for 1616-16, is an item which shews that the chapter paid 
468. Sd. for a through stone of marble, and an inscribed plate of brass to lay 
over dean Harrington. (Fabric Rolls, 97.)

• A younger son of the lordly house of Fitzhugh. Hia father was Henry 
Fitzhngh, his mother Alice, daughter of Richard Neville earl of Salisbury. He 
was pushed forward in life with that scandalous haste which marked the rise of 
so many members of noble families. On the 21st of May, 1475, he was collated 
by his kinsman, archbishop Neville, to the stall of Weighton at York. (Reg. 
Neville, ii. 17 a.) He was at this time only thirteen years of-«gel On April 

27, 1476, Sixtus IV. gave him leave to hold a benefice, when he was sixteen, he 
being of noble birth, and the cousin of Edward IV. (Reg. Geo. Neville.) Fitz- 
hugh, however, it will be seen, had already taken time by the forelock. In 1477, 
when he was fifteen, he had a presentation to tbe rich rectory of fiedale, but it 
was a faulty one and nothing came of it. (Reg. archid. Richmond.) In 1478 
he was admitted B.A. at Cambridge, with liberty to go out M.A. when he would, 
and to be regent or not as he thought fit. In 1483 he was D.D. (Ath. Cant. i. 10 ; 
Hawes' and Loder's Framlingham, 220; Lei. Coll. v. 388). In 1480 he was 
elected master of Pembroke coll. which he held during his life, and in 1496 and 
1501 he was made chancellor of the University. (Le Neve iii. 601.) 

On March 15, 1478-9, he was instituted to the living of Wintrlngham on his 
mother's presentation (MS. Harl. 6952, 103 a), and, on April 18, 1482, he was 
instituted to the rectory of Bingham, Notts. (Reg. Rotherham, 167 J). On Sept. 

28, 1485, he was collated to the prebend at St. Catharine's altar at Beverley 
(Ibid. 1005) which he resigned in 1488. 

His chief preferments were at Lincoln. From 1474-5 to 1477 he was pre- 
bendary of Empingham (Le Neve, ii. 147). In 1486 he became prebendary of 
Croperdy there. (Ibid. ii. 140.) In Oct. 1483, he reached his highest honour, 
the deanery of Lincoln, which he held until his death on November 20th, 1505. 
(Ibid. ii. 33.) He kept a large household (Ath. Cant. i. 522), and along with 
his mother was a contributor to the stock of vestments which belonged to the 
cathedral. (Dugd. Mon. vi. 1279, 1283-5.) 

There ' are some notices of George Fitzhugh in Ath. Cant. i. 10, 622 ; 
Churton's Lives of the Founders of Brasenose College, 121 ; Lei. Coll. v. 388 ; 
Dngdale*s Baronage, i. 405 ; Hist. Univ. Cant. i. 58.

Lancashire, and became firmly rooted in the West Riding. Its headquarters 
were at Bramhope. The testator seems to have been a son of Robert Dyneley of

B.M. at Whitkirk. He makes his wife Agnes and his son William executors, 
and his brother John Dyneley and his cousin Robert Albot superrisors. [Pr. 
Not. 26, 1477.] (Reg. Test. y. 24 b.)

On Jan. 25, 1493-4, Collins was instituted to the rectory of Wilford, Notts.

Cleveland (Beg. Savage, 19a.), and on Dec. 5, 1505, he was collated to the stall 
of Palishall at Southwell. (Ibid. 29a.) On April 12, 1501, and Dec. 3, 1508, 
he was made official of the court of Tork. (Begg. Savage, lb.; and Bain- 
bridge, 1 a.) 

In the cathedral of York Oollins held the following offices : On Nov. 7, 1494, 
he was admitted to the stall of Bugthorpe (Acta Capit. Ebor.), and on Nov. 30 
seq., he was collated to that of Apesthorpe. (Beg. Botherham, 106a.) On Nov. 
18, 1496, Collins was advanced to the dignity of precentor (Ibid. 108 a), the 
prebend of Driffield going with it ; whilst, on Sept. 12, 1503, he was collated to 
the treasurership, in which office he died. (Beg. Savage, 24 a.) 

It will be seen from the present will that Collins was a munificent friend to 
the minster, to which he was bound by so many ties. See Fabric RollSy pp. 
216, 309. 

Collins was buried in York minster, in the position that he had selected for 
himself, under ''a blue marble stone, about four yards long, with the four 
Evangelists in as many cinque -foils at comers ; towards the foot two cscocheous 
of this charge, viz., three martlets on a bend ; and at the head a brass plate " 
bearing an inscription showing that Collins died on Feb. 4, 1508-9. (MS. 
Torre, 162 ; Drake's Eburacum,601.) 

The brother of the testator, John Collins, alias Twyford, was instituted at 
his brother's presentation to the vicarage of St. Mary Bishophill Junior, in 
York, on Oct. 28, 1504. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) Tliis he resigned, on account of old 
age, in 1522, receiving from it an annual pension of 4/. 6«. %d. It is more than 
probable that the two brothers were natives of Twyford, near Melton Mowbray, 
m Leicestershire.

Collins and Thomas Dalby seem to have been the Archbishop's execntors, who 
died on the 3rd of September 1507, but these papers extend over several years 
beyond that date. The grand inventory of the goods of the Archbishop does

Archbishop. My object in printing them here is to place them permanently on

DISPENSATIONS FOR MARRIAGE, MARRIAGE 

LICENCES, ETC. 

In the third volume of the Testamenta, pp. 311-375, there is 
a list of all these documents that are to be found in the Northern 
Registers between 1374 and 1531. I now complete the list by 
adding those which occur in the earlier registers, together with 
a few that were accidentally omitted in their proper places. 

1308, Nov. 29. Licence from the archbishop of York, citing 
letters from Cardinal Berengarias, the papal penancer, for Roger 
de Mannesherth and Petronilla de Kingthorp "quod possint 
simul stare in matrimoniocontracto." — Reg. archiep. Greenfield^ 
i. 90 b. 

1311-12, Feb. 16. Licence from Robert Pickering, canon of 
York .and vicar-general, for John bishop of Lincoln to receive 
the vow of chastity of Alice widow of Sir Richard de Bingham 
knt. — IbicL ii. 146 a. 

« 

1312-13, March 2. Commission from William archbishop 
of York to Richard bishop of Durham to receive the vow of 
chastity of dame AmabiUa widow of Sir Robert de Cleseby, knt. 
Ibid. ii. 176 6; and Reg. Kellaioe^ 75 a. 

1316, Dec. 5. Commission to David " Recreensis episcopus " 
to receive the vow of chastity from Margaret widow of John 
Chaumon of Colton. — Reg, sede vac. 86 b. 

1318-19, Feb. 16. Dispensation sanctioning a marriage that 
has taken place between William son of Nicholas of Melton and 
Christiana his wife, they being cousins. On inquiry the relation- 
ship is thus shown. Anketinus, called the deacon, has a son 
Thomas and a daughter Agnes. Thomas is the father of Ralph,

838 TESTAMENTA 

called the clerk ; Ralph is the father of another Ralph who is 
the sire of Matilda the mother of William. On the other side 
Agnes is the mother of Alexander Paslew who is the father of 
Greoffroj the father of Christiana. A dispensation from John 
XXIL is cited, dated at Avignon, Jan. 13, 1317-18. — Reff. 
archiep. Melton, 275 a. 

1324, Nov. 23. Absolntion of Robert de Ripon, chaplain, 
from a sentence of suspension for three years for celebrating a 
clandestine marriage between Nicholas, the carpenter of Ripon, 
and Isold de Skelton. — Ibid. 82 6. 

1325, Dec. 23. Absolution of Robert de Darleton, chaplain, 
for celebrating a clandestine marriage between Thomas Mor- 
tayn and Margaret Haunsard. — Ibid. 5666.
